history.heading: Steppe empires
paragraphs: The Mongolian steppe was home to successive nomadic empires, including the Xiongnu, who threatened China around 200 BCE, and the Turkic and Uyghur khaganates.

In 1206 Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and took the title Genghis Khan. He and his successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe. His grandson Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in China. The empire facilitated trade along the Silk Road but caused immense destruction.

history.heading: Qing rule and the Mongolian People's Republic
paragraphs: After the Yuan dynasty fell in 1368, the Mongols returned to the steppe. Tibetan Buddhism became widespread in the 16th century. From the late 17th century, Mongolia came under the Manchu Qing dynasty.

When the Qing fell in 1911, Mongolia declared independence under the Bogd Khan, a Buddhist leader. With Soviet support, the Mongolian People's Republic was established in 1924, becoming the world's second communist state. Purges in the 1930s killed tens of thousands, including many Buddhist monks.

history.heading: Democracy
paragraphs: A peaceful democratic revolution in 1990 ended communist rule, and a new constitution was adopted in 1992. Mongolia has since been a democracy, though politics has been marked by corruption scandals and frequent changes of prime minister.

culture.heading: Nomadic heritage
paragraphs: Mongolian is the official language, written in Cyrillic, with the traditional vertical script being revived. Tibetan Buddhism is the main religion, alongside shamanism. Around a quarter of the population still lives as nomadic herders, living in gers (yurts).

The Naadam festival in July celebrates the "three manly games": wrestling, horse racing and archery. Throat singing (khöömei) and the horsehead fiddle (morin khuur) are recognised by UNESCO. Buuz (dumplings) and airag (fermented mare's milk) are traditional.

politics.heading: Parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: Mongolia is a semi-presidential republic with a directly elected president and a prime minister responsible to the State Great Khural (parliament). Squeezed between Russia and China, Mongolia pursues a "third neighbour" policy of building ties with the United States, Japan, South Korea and Europe.

economy.heading: Mining boom
paragraphs: Mining dominates the economy. Mongolia has huge deposits of coal, copper and gold; the Oyu Tolgoi copper and gold mine is one of the largest in the world. Most exports go to China. Livestock herding, with tens of millions of sheep, goats, horses, cattle and camels, remains important, and Mongolia is a major cashmere producer.
Severe winters (dzud) can kill millions of animals. Ulaanbaatar, home to about half the population, suffers from severe winter air pollution. The currency is the tögrög.
